anchors.fact: Thoreau wrote that the wild apples of old pastures, the ones a farmer leaves out as unsalable, are the walker's choicest fruit in late October and early November (W5, W6).
anchors.meaning: What everyone else passes over as not worth gathering is, to the one who walks there, the best thing in the field.

anchors.fact: He wrote that the same apple, brought into the house, often tastes harsh and crabbed, and that one he took from his desk indoors was unexpectedly crude, sour enough to set a squirrel's teeth on edge; indoors you miss the November air, which is its sauce (W7). Thoreau's claim, not a fact about apples.
anchors.meaning: The fear of being brought indoors and turning sour, in someone else's words: nothing in the apple changed, only the room.

anchors.fact: He applied it to himself: one thought for the field, another for the house; his thoughts, like wild apples, were food for walkers and not warranted palatable in the house (W9). He also wrote that "our wild apple is wild only like myself" (W2).
anchors.meaning: The mirror is his own, on the record, not ours: what he was is right in its own air and wrong in someone else's room.

anchors.fact: Thorny pasture apple bushes, he joked, have "no malice, only some malic acid"; when the tree finally rises, it lets the cows that cropped it into its shade (W3, W4). Same pages also use fighting words ("foes", "defeats").
anchors.meaning: Sharp, not angry. Something that held its ground for years and, once grown, let them in to shade and fruit.

anchors.fact: His friend Emerson wrote that Thoreau kept his freedom "at the cost of disappointing the natural expectations of his family and friends" (E2), and counted it "a fault in him that he had no ambition": instead of engineering for all America, "the captain of a huckleberry party" (E6).
anchors.meaning: The cost spoken by someone who loved him, and he meant it ("if, at the end of years, it is still only beans!").

anchors.fact: Emerson's next sentence calls these "foibles, real or apparent", and says Thoreau's study of nature made his friends curious to see the world through his eyes (E7). He was always ready to lead a huckleberry party with the young people he loved (E8).
anchors.meaning: The disappointment and the love sit in the same paragraph; the friend half grants it may only seem a fault.

anchors.fact: Emerson: "He chose to be rich by making his wants few, and supplying them himself." (E4). Emerson also hedged it: "Perhaps he fell into his way of living" (E5, C3).
anchors.meaning: Enough, called riches by the friend who doubted him. Quote Emerson's line as his; "chose on purpose" stays the guest's, not a fact about Thoreau.

anchors.fact: He once tempted a companion, keeping a straight face, with one of the sour apples; once frost and thaw had turned them sweet, "Now we both greedily fill our pockets" (W11, W12). The page doesn't say who brought whom, or when the tease happened.
anchors.meaning: He didn't carry the apples in to convince anyone: the companion was out there with him, where they taste right. (Winter, not October; "cheated" is his word, so it's a tease, not a lesson; never "he brought/took" the companion.)

anchors.fact: The Stone Fence (also Sampson, recorded from 1750) is spirit and cider in roughly equal parts, "originally rum, and then whisky", hard cider preferred (S1). Jerry Thomas's 1862 version: bourbon, sweet cider, "2 or 3 small lumps of ice" (S2).
anchors.meaning: The old country drink the bar made from the apple: the apple arrives as cider. Ours goes the older way, with rum and hard cider (never "the original recipe", C1).

anchors.fact: Wondrich notes that as late as 1869 a bar manual said a tart, full-flavoured crab-apple cider was often preferred to ordinary cider in the Stone Fence (S3, a relay). Thoreau wrote that small, high-coloured wild apples "are thought to make the best cider" (W10), and Oxford says today's best cider apples are high in tannin, sugar and acid (S5).
anchors.meaning: The sharp apple the market skips is what the cider and the old drink wanted, and still want. That's the clause that keeps "still best where it was left" true today (S5 is present tense).

anchors.fact: Wondrich: by the Civil War the Stone Fence was "a ghost of its former self"; Jerry Thomas's 1862 version (if his testimony is to be believed, Wondrich's hedge) was bourbon with sweet, non-alcoholic cider, which Wondrich calls "suave and smooth, but comparatively feeble"; the older drink was hard cider and New England rum (*Imbibe!* pdf 160, S2). **Dates:** the tart crab-apple cider (S3) is 1869, seven years *after* Thomas's 1862 book.
anchors.meaning: The sharp version didn't come before the soft one and vanish: it carried on beside it. Someone in 1869 still preferred the tart cider while the fashionable glass had gone smooth. Never "before it was softened" (wrong order); "feeble" is Wondrich's judgement, credited to him.

anchors.fact: Right before "best cider", Thoreau wrote: "I still begrudge them to the cider-mill" (W10). He drank no wine (E10); nothing says he drank cider.
anchors.meaning: Own it in one clause if the reading names cider at all: he'd rather have eaten them in the field. Never "Thoreau's drink".

cocktail.closingLine: Carry it out of doors before you taste it. Whoever follows you out will understand.
cocktail.glassware: a heavy tumbler (about 300 ml), two or three small lumps of ice
method: Keep the cider cold in the fridge until you need it.
Drop two or three small lumps of ice into a heavy tumbler and pour in the rum.
Pour the cider in slowly over the ice, and give it one turn with a spoon.
Cut one thin slice from the sharpest apple you have, skin on, and slip it into the glass last.
cocktail.name: Fresh Air

recipe.note: rum was the Stone Fence's original spirit, before whisky

recipe.item: dry, still farmhouse cider, the sharpest you can find (about 5-6%)
recipe.note: not sweet, not sparkling. Small, sharp wild apples were thought to make the best cider, Thoreau wrote, though he still begrudged them to the cider-mill
as Jerry Thomas asked for in 1862

recipe.item: raw sharp apple, skin on (a crab apple, or the sourest apple to hand)
recipe.note: the apple he'd rather have eaten in the field: raw, cut last

cocktail.tagline: You know what enough feels like, and make it look like freedom.

reading.epigraph: In 1862 a famous bar book printed this drink with sweet cider. Others kept pouring it tart.
whoYouAre: At a wedding or a birthday, someone asks what you're up to these days. You tell them: the same place, the work you like, your usual walk in the morning. Then you watch them wait politely for the rest. There isn't any rest. Years ago you stepped out of the race everyone else is running, quietly, and you don't miss it.

Living with less was easy. Being loved by people who think you're wasting yourself is harder. "You could do so much more." They mean it kindly, which is why you don't argue. And under that sits a quieter fear. No one will drag you back in. But someone kind might ask, with a job you'd be good at or a favour "just for a while", and once you're back indoors, the part of you they liked would turn sour.

Your way does something for people, and someone should tell you. After an afternoon with you, they go home wanting a little less, and lighter for it. You make "enough" look like a choice, not a defeat, and you show them someone can say no and stay kind.
yours: In late autumn, the writer Henry David Thoreau went into old pastures for the small, sharp apples farmers left out as unsalable. To someone out walking, he wrote, they were the choicest fruit. Indoors, he wrote, it tasted like another fruit: one he took out of his desk was "sour enough to set a squirrel's teeth on edge". There, he wrote, you miss the November air, "which is the sauce it is to be eaten with".

He knew he was describing himself: "one thought for the field, another for the house". His friend Emerson couldn't help "counting it a fault in him that he had no ambition": instead of engineering for all America, he was "the captain of a huckleberry party". Emerson meant it. In the same sketch, Emerson also wrote: "He chose to be rich by making his wants few, and supplying them himself."

As Thoreau tells it, nothing in the apple changes when it's carried in. Only the room does. You know that about yourself, so you keep turning down the bigger room, however kindly it's offered. Emerson wrote that it cost Thoreau nothing to say no. It costs you something every time, because you like the people asking. You're not hiding from anyone. You simply know where you're at your best. And I like to think the ones asking are curious about the world as you see it, and don't know how to say so.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Stone Fence, a drink from colonial America, on record under another name by 1750. I went back to its older pairing of rum and hard cider, and kept it sharp: aged rum and a dry, still farmhouse cider, the sharpest you can find, over two or three small lumps of ice, with no sugar to soften it, because sharp was never a fault that needed fixing. Thoreau wrote that wild apples like his were thought to make the best cider, though he still begrudged them to the cider mill. So, for the apples he'd rather have eaten in the field, a thin slice of raw, sharp apple goes in at the end.

You don't owe anyone a bigger life, or an explanation of this one. Thoreau once kept a smooth face while tempting a companion with one of those sour apples. By winter, when frost and thaw had turned them sweet, the two of them were filling their pockets together. So stop defending your life to the ones who worry about you. Have one of them come along. Some will taste what you taste, and you'll have someone to fill your pockets with.
